text: Seven more, a sentence or two each. The four pillars of OOP. Encapsulation bundles data with its methods and hides the state. Inheritance reuses and specializes a class. Polymorphism gives one call the right behavior for each type. Abstraction shows what an object does, not how. Encapsulation, concretely: an account hides its balance and changes it only through methods that check, so no withdrawal can overdraw it. Guard every way in, the constructor too. An account that opens at minus fifty is overdrawn already. Polymorphism, by example: total area asks each shape for its own area, a circle and a square alike, with no ladder of type checks. A factory centralizes creation, so callers ask for what they want, like a parser for CSV, not how to build it. It pays off when the class depends on runtime input, or construction is complex. A singleton is one instance with a global access point, like a config. It's controversial as global mutable state: it hides dependencies, and a test that passes alone can fail after one that changed the config. A module-level value or plain injection is often cleaner. An interface declares what methods a type must provide, with no implementation. An abstract class can also share code and state. Use an interface for a pure contract, and an abstract class when subclasses share code. And is-a versus has-a. A car is a vehicle: inheritance. A car has an engine: composition. Make car extend engine, and it inherits the engine's whole interface. Ask which it is before you inherit. Every answer here assumed you were the one writing the code. Most of the code you'll be asked about, you didn't write. Next: reading and reviewing code.
